title: Howard the Duck
edition: Willard Huyck’s 111-minute 1986 live-action feature with Lea Thompson.
synopsis: Stranded in Cleveland, Howard finds a friend in Beverly and a possible route home. The same technology opens Earth to an invader.
verdictRationale: Howard has good reason to want his old life back. He gives up the way home when other lives depend on it. That costly choice deserves admiration. The film also regularly invites viewers to laugh at sexual embarrassment and leering. Its last act offers a clearer example of charity than much of its comedy.
ageRationale: Beverly discovers a condom in Howard’s wallet during a bedroom joke. A scientist’s transformation and fights involving gunfire add a different kind of intensity. A teen audience is better placed to discuss both.
reflection: Jennings first treats Howard as someone with a home to miss. Later Howard has to recognize that the people around him have homes to lose, too. Families might consider whose ordinary life they would interrupt their own plans to protect.

themes.name: Self-sacrifice
themes.evidence: Giving up the way back to his planet costs Howard his original goal and settles the final conflict.

themes.name: Hospitality
themes.evidence: Beverly befriends the stranded visitor and Jennings tries to send him home. Welcoming Howard sets the adventure in motion before the rescue takes over.

themes.name: Sexualized humor
themes.evidence: An adult magazine gag and the bedroom encounter recur as comedy. They shape the tone, while Howard’s final decision turns on another concern.

themes.name: LGBTQ Themes & Messaging
themes.evidence: The guide documents Beverly and Howard’s flirtation. Screen the 111-minute feature for additional relationships, dialogue and background details before assigning prominence.

title: Captain America
edition: Albert Pyun’s standard release with Matt Salinger and Scott Paulin, identified by the bomb and recording in the castle finale.
synopsis: Decades after a wartime mission, Steve Rogers returns to a country he barely recognizes. Sharon helps him trace the Red Skull through an Italian diary and a recording made in the villain’s childhood home.
verdictRationale: Sharon has just lost her mother, yet she uses her knowledge of Italian and risks capture to help others. Steve twice tries to leave a helper behind and finally uses a childhood trauma to distract his enemy. The rescue is courageous. The means Steve uses make his example a complicated one for families.
ageRationale: Soldiers interrupt a child’s piano recital and kill his family in front of him. The sounds of that killing return during the climax. A child sensitive to the loss of a parent may find the recording harder to hear than the later action is to watch.
reflection: Sharon has every reason to withdraw after Bernice dies. Instead, she listens, translates and goes back when Steve leaves her behind. A Christian family might ask what it costs to receive another person’s help when one is accustomed to being the rescuer.

themes.name: Service and courage
themes.evidence: Sharon translates the diary and later risks capture. Her choices repeatedly make the rescue possible.

themes.name: Coercion
themes.evidence: The child taken from his family grows into the man who plans to control a president with an implant. Coercion binds the origin and the central plot together.

themes.name: Deceit
themes.evidence: Steve uses the same trick on two allies to obtain a car and leave them behind. Sharon has to find her own way to the village.

themes.name: LGBTQ Themes & Messaging
themes.evidence: Sharon’s relationship with Steve covers one story thread. Check dialogue and incidental characters throughout the standard release before scoring.
